final_answer:
Merge sort operates as a divide-and-conquer algorithm, breaking down a list into smaller sublists until each sublist contains a single element. These sublists are then merged back together in a sorted manner. The process involves recursively splitting the list into two halves until the base case (a single element) is reached. Once the list is divided, the merging phase begins. During this phase, adjacent sublists are combined by comparing the elements at the front of each sublist and appending the smaller element to a new sorted list. This process continues until all elements are merged into a single sorted list. The merging step ensures that the final combined list is sorted, as each sublist is already sorted from the recursive division.

Merge sort is preferred over quicksort for linked lists due to the nature of linked list data structures. Quicksort relies on efficient random access to elements, which is inefficient in linked lists because accessing the nth element requires traversing from the head, resulting in O(n) time complexity. In contrast, merge sort’s divide step can be implemented efficiently in linked lists using a slow-and-fast pointer technique to locate the midpoint, which operates in O(n) time. Additionally, merge sort’s merge operation is well-suited for linked lists, as it can be performed in O(1) space by adjusting pointers rather than requiring additional memory for copying elements. This makes merge sort more space-efficient for linked lists compared to quicksort, which may require more memory for partitioning. Furthermore, merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases, while quicksort’s worst-case performance degrades to O(n²), which is less desirable for linked lists where worst-case scenarios are harder to avoid.
